title: 11 examples of YouTube influencer marketing
summary: Level up your YouTube presence with the help of these 11 YouTube influencer marketing examples. Explore popular formats, why they work and how to use them.
body_text: Table of Contents Share Email Share Resource If you’re not already partnering with YouTube influencers, it’s time to change that. Sprout Social’s 2026 Content Strategy Report revealed that consumers are increasingly turning to YouTube to inform their buying behavior. Approximately 24% find new products on the network, with consumers almost as likely to seek out product education as they are entertainment. And YouTube influencers have a powerful role to play in both spaces. With built-in audiences of thousands or millions, influencers on YT have a unique ability to build awareness, demonstrate real-world value and spark lasting interest. When you leverage YouTube influencer marketing , you’re backing your brand with the network’s most trusted voices. To help you get started, we’ve rounded up 10 YouTube influencer marketing examples, why they work and how to use them for your business. 1. Unboxing Unboxing involves opening new products on camera, showcasing packaging and features. Oftentimes, creators simultaneously share their first impressions on look, feel and functionality to give viewers a better idea of what to expect. That’s what Marques Brownlee did when he unboxed the iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone Air on his YouTube channel. Upon opening the products, he compared their designs and battery capabilities, then provided his hot take on the models—a piece of intrigue he strategically included in the title. When and why it works Unboxing content is ideal for product-based brands in sectors like technology, beauty and fashion. They’re the perfect format for highly anticipated launches, especially when led by influencers. Creators often receive products before the average consumer, meaning their videos provide the first sneak peek at what’s inside the box. This early access creates hype around a product and fosters a sense of exclusivity; viewers feel like they’re part of a moment they can’t experience anywhere else. And even if they don’t get the products pre-launch, their content can still help increase awareness over time and convert consumers on the fence. 2. Tutorials and how-tos Most YouTube influencer marketing campaigns aren’t complete without how-to content. As the name suggests, these videos see creators provide step-by-step guidance on how to perform a specific process, whether it’s changing a tire or perfecting a smoky eye. With the right expertise, influencers can lend credibility and increase consumer confidence. With over two million subscribers and several years of experience as a makeup artist, UK influencer Lisa Eldridge offers an impactful mix of skill and reputation. Her buy-in instantly makes products feel more professional, reliable and worth investing in. When and why it works Users love tutorials for their practicality and accessibility. They learn new skills on a free platform and in a format they can stop, start and rewatch as many times as needed. For brands, tutorials don’t just promote products but actively teach consumers how to use them. This is ideal for consumers in the awareness and consideration phases because it helps them understand the product’s purpose, see it in action and build confidence before buying. 3. Product reviews In this style of YouTube content, creators share their overall impressions of specific products, listing pros, cons and key considerations for their audience. While these videos carry some similarities with unboxings, they’re generally more comprehensive in rating the item’s overall quality. For example, health influencer Doctor Mike shared a taste-test video on his channel featuring fellow influencers Joe Santagato and Frankie Alvarez, with the trio rating viral protein snacks. And since not every product receives glowing feedback, the ones that do stand out even more in consumers’ minds. When and why it works Much like traditional reviews and testimonials, product review videos can be a valuable form of social proof . They give your audience insight into how other consumers feel about your business—in their words. A positive review could ease a consumer’s hesitation in the consideration phase and nudge them towards conversion. Plus, brands don’t necessarily need exclusivity to stand out in product reviews, making them more versatile and suitable for brands of various sizes and budgets. 4. Get ready with me (GRWM) GRWM videos are one of the top influencer marketing trends in 2026. Creators film themselves performing their daily grooming routines while talking directly to the camera or via voiceover. YouTuber lay luv is proof that GRWMs aren’t reserved for mega-influencers heading to red-carpet events. She’s found success sharing her preparation process for an average day of high school—making her extremely relatable, especially with young audiences. When and why it works GRWM videos are a goldmine for natural product integration, particularly from brands in the cosmetic, skincare, fragrance and fashion industries. Because these items slot seamlessly into influencers’ everyday routines, they feel like authentic recommendations rather than overt product placements. 5. Makeover transformations Another effective form of YouTube influencer marketing is makeover content. This entails creators revamping a particular space—be it their kitchen, office or backyard—using a brand’s products. Lone Fox—aka Drew Michael Scott—is a popular home design and DIY YouTuber who regularly shares makeover content. Whether it’s a living room refresh or a closet declutter, he takes his audience along for the ride as he transforms a space, then wows them with the before-and-after. When and why it works Makeover content is ideal for brands that specialize in furniture, household appliances or home decor. These products thrive on visual impact—and few formats convey that better than a before-and-after reveal. Not to mention, makeovers also tap into a content framework that viewers love: progress. Makeovers rarely happen overnight; usually, it’s a slow and steady unfolding that builds towards a major transformation. This lends itself well to episodic content series , which is becoming increasingly popular among social users for the predictability and connection it provides. Per Sprout’s Q2 2025 Pulse Survey, 57% of users want brands to actively prioritize this content. 6. Contests and giveaways Contests and giveaways see brands partner with creators to gift viewers products or services. In exchange for providing free goods or services, brands get increased visibility and awareness. Take MrBeast, who often holds large-scale giveaways on his channel. On one occasion, he gifted 50 subscribers with brand-new laptops—and offered some high-level exposure for the brands backing the technology, Lenovo and Intel. When and why it works Giveaways are highly versatile, making them suitable for brands across industries. Whether it’s a one-year software subscription or a limited-edition product, every business provides some form of value that can double as a prize. Most contests offer low-effort entry; to partake, users only have to follow an account, like a post or leave a comment. This is particularly impactful for consumers in the awareness stage because it ensures that their first touchpoint with your company is all value, no cost. Even if they don’t win, they’ll remember your business as something worth winning and one that gives to its community. 7. Silent reviews and aesthetic montages In some YouTube influencer marketing campaigns, saying nothing says it all. Silent reviews and aesthetic montages involve no talking. Instead, creators use facial expressions and gestures, text overlay, sound effects or visuals to captivate and communicate. Take this silent book review from Ireland-based YouTuber Bookgirlnextdoor. In it, she gives her honest opinions on popular novels—without uttering a single word. When and why it works In general, silent reviews and montages are best suited to products with high visual or sensory appeal—think beauty, skincare, homewares and fashion. But brands outside these industries can still get in on the fun, with a silent book review being a key example. It subverts expectations by turning a typically verbal format into something totally silent. Because the delivery is untraditional, it feels fresh and captivating—which can help drive brand interest and engagement. 8. Challenges and stunts A popular niche on YouTube sees influencers perform or coordinate high-risk, unconventional or extreme feats. Oftentimes, these tasks are gamified, making the content even more entertaining for viewers. Aussie YouTubers Brett Stanford, Derek Herron and Scott Gaunson have leveraged stunt-based content to build a following of millions. On their channel, you’ll regularly see them attempting outlandish challenges, such as launching a giant frisbee off a cliff or trying to crush a car using only water . When and why it works This content sees people testing their limits, trying new things and redefining what’s possible. So, it’s a great fit for brands that do the same. Companies built around adventure and innovation slot seamlessly into challenge videos because their ethos matches the premise of the video. As a result, their integration feels organic, not forced. 9. Hauls In haul videos, creators show off items they recently purchased, either from one or multiple retailers. For instance, Irish influencer Sophie Murray focused on a single retailer in a haul posted to her YouTube channel: H&M. As she showed off each product, she discussed key details—such as sizing and pricing—and included B-roll of her wearing it. When and why it works Whether it’s fashion, beauty, technology or homewares, hauls are best suited to product-based brands due to the content’s “show-and-tell” format. They’re also ideal for consumers in the consideration phase who want to see products up close before buying. Additionally, many creators—like Sophie—feature affiliate marketing links in their video descriptions to facilitate conversion. 10. Day in the life Day-in-the-life content gives viewers an authentic, intimate look at an influencer’s day, documenting everything from work to relationships to hobbies. French influencer Shera takes her two million subscribers through her everyday life in her vlogs. In the one below, she captures how she balances her personal life (i.e. raising her children) and professional life (i.e. running a business) in a 24-hour period. When and why it works Making breakfast, running errands, putting the kids to bed—day-in-the-life content taps into the relatability of everyday life. And relatability is an invaluable currency for brands. Per the 2025 Sprout Social Index™ , consumers crave authenticity and relatability from brands on social more than anything else. Because they have high levels of audience trust, influencers can dial that resonance up even further. When they show how a product or service fits into their routine, it helps viewers visualize how it could slot into their lives. 11. Parodies and creative skits These videos involve creators acting out fictional scenarios, usually in a comedic or satirical way that pokes fun at a particular topic or trend. Because they’re typically short-form, skits are ideal for YouTube Shorts . YouTube influencer Ryan George is known for his tongue-in-cheek skits, which cover a wide range of topics. Whether it’s AI, pop culture or unspoken social rules, he can find a comedic spin for just about anything. When and why it works Punchy and playful, skits are highly captivating and versatile. Creators like Ryan are skilled at finding the funny side of any product or service—including the ones you offer. With their humor, you can hook people in the awareness stage instantly and start familiarizing them with your brand. From there, you can subtly and comedically educate them on the specific pain points your business addresses for them. Key brand takeaways from examples of YouTube influencer marketing Now that you’ve seen examples of YouTuber influencer marketing in action, let’s take a look at the most important insights to inform your strategy: 1. The “first 60 seconds” rule While long-form content is king on YouTube, you still need to cater to short attention spans. Make sure your hook (i.e. the first 60 seconds) is compelling enough to entice viewers to stick around. Open your video with a thought-provoking question. Piece together several high-energy, short-form clips from the video in a trailer-style format to give viewers a sneak peek at what’s to come. Display bold animated text on the screen that immediately piques people’s interest. 2. Integrated product utility over product placements It’s not enough for your products or services to simply appear in a video—audiences want to see real, practical examples of how they’ll fit into their lives. In other words, show don’t tell. Demonstrating your product in action is the best way to underscore its value and emphasize the problem you’re solving. 3. Partner with influencers aligned to your brand identity If an influencer’s values and aesthetics don’t align with your brand’s, your messaging won’t resonate. Even worse, you could erode audience trust or damage your credibility. Sprout Social Influencer Marketing ensure you’re collaborating with the right creators. For instance, the Brand Fit Score quantifies how a creator’s audience and content coincide with your brand. Or, you can use Recruit to create a branded application page and let influencers come to you. 4. Optimize for social media search Users are actively using social networks as search engines and YouTube is the OG network for social search. Optimize your YouTube account for social media search by creating dedicated videos specifically geared towards long-tail keyword queries. While broad search terms may garner larger monthly search volumes, the competition is also higher. By targeting long-tail keywords, you can narrow down your audience to high-intent users. For example, instead of making a video titled “how to make coffee”, consider a more niche option like “how to make a cookie butter iced latte without an espresso machine”. 5. Multi-platform repurposing multiplies ROI Repurposing social media content for multiple platforms is an excellent way to maintain cross-channel consistency, build share of voice and strengthen ROI. Make the most of your long-form YouTube videos by extracting the most compelling moments in short-form clips. You can then share these across various formats and networks, such as YouTube Shorts, TikTok and Instagram Reels—turning one piece of content into multiple social touchpoints. 6. Comments are a goldmine for real-time research and development Audience feedback is one of the most valuable tools for content refinement—and your comment section is brimming with these insights. Use Sprout Listening to scan your comments regularly to understand what viewers enjoy, what they want to see more of or issues they’re having (e.g. broken description links). Then, use this data to guide your future content initiatives. Invest in collaborations for even stronger results With the right collaborators, your YouTube presence can become an engine for awareness, engagement and long-term retention. By applying these YouTube influencer marketing examples to your business, you’ll meet your audience at every stage of the consumer journey. And when you choose creators whose audiences and values align with yours, driving awareness and deepening trust becomes even easier. With Sprout Influencer Marketing, finding those perfect-fit creators and managing influencer campaigns is simple. Schedule a demo today to explore these features firsthand. Frequently asked questions Which format drives the most actual sales? Product reviews and tutorials typically drive the most sales because they target consumers later in the buyer journey. These viewers are actively researching and comparing product options, making them more likely to convert after watching. How do we stop viewers from skipping the sponsored part of a vlog? Weave it into the narrative. Instead of a forced 30-second spiel about why your product is great, incorporate it into the story the video is telling. Should brands give creators a strict script for a review? No. While you can give them key talking points as a high-level guide, let them say things in their own voice. Otherwise, the partnership will feel unnatural and fail to resonate with their audiences. body_text: Recently, our CEO had the opportunity to visit our El Monte, California, site, where we manufacture strain gauges and force-torque sensors. The visit reinforced something we believe strongly: Innovation doesn’t end when we design a product. Real impact comes when we can scale that innovation. Our force-torque sensors are enabling some of the most exciting applications in robotics today, including humanoid robots, minimally invasive and robotic surgery, and advanced automation. These technologies allow robots to better understand and interact with the physical world through highly precise force and touch sensing. After several years of planning and execution, we’ve successfully completed the first phase of automation and validated the next phase, creating a strong foundation for future growth. Scaling manufacturing is a critical part of our strategy. It enables us to increase capacity, improve efficiency and reduce costs while maintaining the precision and quality our customers expect. As physical AI continues to accelerate, technologies like these will play an increasingly important role in making robots more capable, adaptable and safe. None of this happens without exceptional teamwork. The progress we’re seeing in El Monte reflects the collaboration of employees across operations, engineering and manufacturing who have worked together to turn a long-term vision into reality. It’s exciting to see that vision becoming operational, and even more exciting to think about what’s next.

body_text: P3 Health Partners Announces Second Quarter 2026 Results August 10, 2026 4:05pm EDT Download as PDF Related Documents Audio Earnings Webcast 10-Q Filing PDF HTML XBRL ZIP HTML Raises Full-Year 2026 Adjusted EBITDA Guidance Management to Host Conference Call and Webcast August 10, 2026 at 4:30 PM ET HENDERSON, Nev.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- P3 Health Partners Inc. (“P3” or the “Company”) (NASDAQ: PIII), a patient-centered and physician-led population health management company, today announced its financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. "Q2 demonstrates that the business is now executing according to our plan. We delivered $54 million of adjusted EBITDA, with the core business driving improved profitability quarter over quarter. Our results reflect the structural improvements now embedded across our contracts, our network, and our operating model, the work I outlined at the onset of my tenure. That strength gives us the confidence to raise our full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA outlook and to enter the second half focused on execution," said Dr. Aric Coffman, CEO of P3. Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results At-risk membership was approximately 105,000 members for the second quarter, a decrease of 10% compared to prior year, reflecting previously disclosed intentional network and payer rationalization. Total lives under management were approximately 133,000 for the quarter, including approximately 28,000 lives under management service arrangements. Total revenue was $386 million, an increase of 9% compared with the prior year quarter. Total per-member capitated revenue increased 15% from the same period in the prior year driven by improved network economics, rate progression, and burden of illness performance. Medical margin(1) for the quarter was $97.8 million, or $311 on a per-member-per-month basis. The results include the favorable impact of payer settlements and prior year development recognized in the quarter. Excluding these items, medical margin for the quarter was $52.9 million, or $168 on a per-member-per-month basis. Net income was $15.7 million compared to a net loss of $43.7 million in the prior year quarter. Adjusted EBITDA(1) for the quarter was $54.4 million, or $173 per-member-per-month, compared to a loss of $17.1 million, or negative $49 per-member-per-month in the prior year quarter. Revised Fiscal 2026 Guidance Full-year revised guidance reflects the impact of underlying first half performance, as well as the prior-year development and payer settlements recognized in the quarter. Year Ending December 31, 2026 Low High At-risk Members(2) 102,000 106,000 Total Revenues (in millions) $1,500 $1,600 Medical Margin(1)(3) (in millions) $260 $300 Medical Margin(1)(3) PMPM $210 $240 Adjusted EBITDA(1)(3) (in millions) $80 $110 (1) Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA per member, per month (“PMPM”), medical margin, and medical margin PMPM are non-GAAP financial measures. For reconciliations of these measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures, if applicable, and more information regarding the Company’s use of non-GAAP financial measures, please see the section titled “Non-GAAP Financial Measures.” (2) See “Key Performance Metrics” for additional information on how the Company defines “at-risk members.” (3) The Company is not able to provide a quantitative reconciliation of guidance for Adjusted EBITDA, medical margin and medical margin PMPM to net income (loss), gross profit and gross profit PMPM, the most directly comparable GAAP measures, respectively, and has not provided forward-looking guidance for net income (loss), because of the uncertainty around certain items that may impact net income (loss), gross profit (loss) or gross profit (loss) PMPM that are not within our control or cannot be reasonably predicted without unreasonable effort. For more information regarding the non-GAAP financial measures discussed in this press release, please see “Non-GAAP Financial Measures” below. The foregoing 2026 outlook statement represents management's current estimate as of the date of this release. Actual results may differ materially depending on a number of factors. Investors are urged to read the “Cautionary Note Regarding Forward-Looking Statements” included in this release. Management does not assume any obligation to update these estimates. Management to Host Conference Call and Webcast on August 10, 2026 at 4:30 PM ET Title & Webcast P3 Health Second Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call Date & Time August 10, 2026, 4:30 PM Eastern Time Conference Call Details Toll-Free 1-833-316-0546 (US) International 1-412-317-0692 Ask to be joined into the P3 Health Partners call The conference call will also be webcast live in the “Events & Presentations” section of the Investor page of the P3 website ( ir.p3hp.org ). The Company’s press release will be available on the Investor page of P3’s website in advance of the conference call. An archived recording of the webcast will be available on the Investor page of P3’s website for a period of 90 days following the conference call. About P3 Health Partners (NASDAQ: PIII): P3 Health Partners Inc. is a leading population health management company committed to transforming healthcare by improving the lives of both patients and providers. Founded and led by physicians, P3 has an expansive network of more than 2,100 affiliated primary care providers across the country. Our local teams of health care professionals manage the care of thousands of patients in 26 counties across five states. P3 supports primary care providers with value-based care coordination and administrative services that improve patient outcomes and lower costs. Through partnerships with these local providers, the P3 care team creates an enhanced patient experience by navigating, coordinating, and integrating the patient’s care within the healthcare system. For more information, visit www.p3hp.org and follow us on LinkedIn and Facebook.com/p3healthpartners . Non-GAAP Financial Measures In addition to the financial results prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the U.S. (“GAAP”), this press release contains certain non-GAAP financial measures as defined by the SEC rules, including Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA PMPM, medical margin, medical margin PMPM, and adjusted operating expense. EBITDA is defined as GAAP net income (loss) before (i) interest, (ii) income taxes and (iii) depreciation and amortization. Adjusted EBITDA is defined as EBITDA, further adjusted to exclude the effect of certain supplemental adjustments, such as (i) mark-to-market warrant gain/loss, (ii) premium deficiency reserves, (iii) equity-based compensation expense, (iv) certain transaction and other related costs and (v) certain other items that we believe are not indicative of our core operating performances. Adjusted EBITDA PMPM is defined as Adjusted EBITDA divided by the number of at-risk Medicare members each month divided by the number of months in the period. We believe these non-GAAP financial measures provide an additional tool for investors to use in evaluating ongoing operating results and trends and in comparing our financial measures with other similar companies. Medical margin represents the amount earned from capitation revenue after medical claims expenses are deducted and medical margin PMPM is defined as medical margin divided by the number of Medicare members each month divided by the number of months in the period. Medical claims expenses represent costs incurred for medical services provided to our members. As our platform grows and matures over time, we expect medical margin to increase in absolute dollars; however, medical margin PMPM may vary as the percentage of new members brought onto our platform fluctuates. New membership added to the platform is typically dilutive to medical margin PMPM. Adjusted operating expense is defined as total operating expense excluding depreciation and amortization and costs that management believes are non-core to the underlying operations of the Company, consisting of (i) medical expense, (ii) premium deficiency reserves, (iii) equity-based compensation, and (iv) certain other items that we believe are not indicative of our core operating performance. We do not consider these non-GAAP measures in isolation or as an alternative to financial measures determined in accordance with GAAP. These non-GAAP financial measures are subject to inherent limitations as they reflect the exercise of judgments by management about which expense and income are excluded or included in determining these non-GAAP financial measures. In addition, other companies may calculate non-GAAP financial measures differently or may use other measures to evaluate their performance, all of which could reduce the usefulness of our non-GAAP financial measures as tools for comparison. The tables at the end of this press release present a reconciliation of Adjusted EBITDA, medical margin to gross profit, medical margin PMPM to gross profit PMPM, and adjusted operating expense to operating expense, which are the most directly comparable financial measures calculated in accordance with GAAP. Key Performance Metrics In addition to our GAAP and non-GAAP financial information, the Company also monitors “at-risk members” to help us evaluate our business, identify trends affecting our business, formulate business plans and make strategic decisions. At-risk membership represents the approximate number of Medicare members for whom we receive a fixed percentage of premium under capitation arrangements as of the end of a particular period. title: Scully Royalty Ltd. board of directors adopts Advance Notice Policy for director nominations
body_text: Policy Establishes Transparent Process and Disclosure Requirements for Shareholder Director Nominations New York (August 10, 2026): Scully Royalty Ltd. (NYSE: SRL) (the "Company") today announced that its Board of Directors (the "Board") has adopted a supplemental Advance Notice Policy (the "Policy"), effective immediately. The Policy has been adopted in furtherance of, and pursuant to the authority granted under, the Company's Amended and Restated Memorandum and Articles of Association (the "Articles"). The Policy establishes a transparent, orderly and structured process for shareholder nominations of directors, consistent with the Articles and applicable law. The Policy is intended to ensure that the Company and its shareholders receive timely, complete and accurate information regarding any person proposed for election to the Board and the shareholder or shareholders proposing such nominee. Among other things, the Policy requires nominating shareholders and proposed nominees to provide information necessary for the Company to assess compliance with the Company's governing documents and applicable law, the eligibility and qualifications of proposed nominees, and matters that may be material to shareholders' understanding of a nominee's experience, independence or suitability to serve as a director. The full text of the Policy will be made available on the Company's website and filed with the Company's public disclosure documents. The Policy may be amended, modified or repealed by the Board at any time, subject to the Articles and applicable law. The Board may waive any requirement of the Policy only to the extent permitted by the Articles and applicable law. About Scully Royalty Ltd. Scully Royalty Ltd. (NYSE: SRL) holds a net revenues royalty interest on the Scully Iron Ore Mine located in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada. It also holds various merchant banking and industrial interests globally. For more information, visit www.scullyroyalty.com . title: Universal Health Services, Inc. Completes Acquisition of Talkspace, Inc.
summary: Creates nation's first full continuum of behavioral healthcare services, supporting people across every stage of their mental health journey.
body_text: Newsroom , Press , Timeline August 17, 2026 Universal Health Services, Inc. Completes Acquisition of Talkspace, Inc. UHS_Talkspace_logo Creates nation’s first full continuum of behavioral healthcare services, supporting people across every stage of their mental health journey. King of Prussia, PA and New York, NY (August 17, 2026) — Universal Health Services, Inc. (NYSE: UHS) today announced the successful completion of its acquisition of Talkspace, Inc. (NASDAQ: TALK), bringing together one of the nation’s largest providers of healthcare services with a leading virtual behavioral health platform to redefine how mental healthcare is accessed and delivered. Talkspace’s virtual care platform complements UHS’ extensive network of affiliated behavioral health facilities, acute care hospitals and outpatient locations, creating an end-to-end behavioral health ecosystem that connects care across settings and levels of need.* By making transitions between levels of care more seamless – from virtual support, counseling, therapy and psychiatry to outpatient programs, crisis intervention, inpatient treatment and specialized care – the combined offerings position the organization moving forward to support patients throughout their mental health journey. “We’re at an inflection point in how mental healthcare is delivered,” said Marc D. Miller, President and CEO of UHS. “People deserve a system that is easy to navigate, connected across care settings and built around their evolving needs. The addition of Talkspace expands our ability to connect people with care when, where and how they need it most. And we are strengthening the connection between behavioral and physical health for overall wellbeing.” Talkspace serves individuals across all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico through a network of approximately 6,000 licensed providers whose services are currently available to more than 200 million people through health insurance plans, employers, employee assistance programs, schools and government organizations. Talkspace also offers self-pay options. Talkspace recently introduced Tee , its AI-powered, purpose-built mental health guide developed to meet HIPAA privacy standards and provide subscribers with real-time support and feedback. Tee can assist individuals between appointments or as a standalone supportive companion. “Joining UHS allows us to accelerate the mission that has guided Talkspace from the beginning: making high-quality mental healthcare more accessible to more people,” said Jon R. Cohen, MD, CEO of Talkspace. “Together, we’re excited to create a nationwide network of care that brings virtual, outpatient and inpatient care together to better support patients, clinicians and communities.” As demand for behavioral health services continues to grow, the combined organization is positioned to offer patients greater flexibility and choice while improving care coordination across settings. The integrated model also strengthens support for employers, health plans and community partners seeking scalable, evidence-based mental healthcare solutions. The transaction was originally announced on March 9, 2026, and has now received all necessary regulatory approvals and satisfied customary closing conditions. The companies will begin working together immediately to thoughtfully integrate capabilities while ensuring uninterrupted service for patients, providers and partners. * Treating practitioners are individually licensed and exercise independent professional judgment in diagnosing and treating patients consistent with their training, scope of practice and licensure. About UHS Headquartered in King of Prussia, PA, Universal Health Services, Inc. (NYSE: UHS) is one of the nation’s largest and most respected providers of hospital and healthcare services, with annual revenues of approximately $17.4 billion during 2025. Through its subsidiaries, UHS employs more than 101,500 individuals and operates 30 inpatient acute care facilities, more than 380 inpatient behavioral health facilities and approximately 170 outpatient and other facilities across 40 states, Washington, D.C., Puerto Rico, Ireland and the United Kingdom. Through its subsidiaries, UHS also offers an insurance offering, a physician network and various related services in the United States. Since our founding in 1979, UHS has grown steadily into a premier Fortune 500® corporation perennially recognized by multiple esteemed national rating entities. Our strategy includes investing in talented staff, facilities, technology and innovation across broad care continuums to deliver favorable patient outcomes and contribute to the overall health and wellbeing of the patients we are privileged to serve. A wholly-owned subsidiary of UHS also acts as the advisor to Universal Health Realty Income Trust, a real estate investment trust (NYSE: UHT). About Talkspace, a Universal Health Services, Inc. Subsidiary Talkspace , a Universal Health Services, Inc. subsidiary, is a leading virtual behavioral healthcare provider committed to helping people lead healthier, happier lives through access to high-quality mental healthcare. Through its subsidiaries and affiliates, Talkspace offers a comprehensive suite of mental health services – including therapy for individuals, teens and couples as well as psychiatry and medication management. Among its offerings is Tee, a standalone, clinician-informed AI mental health guide available to those 18+ for 24/7 behavioral support. With Talkspace’s core therapy offerings, members are matched with one of thousands of affiliated licensed therapists within days and can engage in live video, audio or chat sessions, and/or unlimited asynchronous text messaging sessions. title: Radiopharmaceutical Development: How Strong Preclinical Strategy Builds Translational Confidence
summary: Explore how integrated preclinical radiopharmaceutical studies using PDX models, imaging, biodistribution, dosimetry, and efficacy data can build translational confidence earlier.
body_text: Radiopharmaceutical Development Is Accelerating, and Preclinical Decisions Matter More Than Ever Radiopharmaceutical development is advancing at a pace that would have been difficult to imagine even a few years ago. The 2022 approval of Pluvicto as the first targeted radioligand therapy for PSMA-positive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer was a defining moment for the field, helping to validate the clinical potential of radiopharmaceuticals and accelerate broader investment, innovation, and sponsor interest in this modality. New isotopes, targeting vectors, linker chemistries, and therapeutic concepts are expanding what is possible in oncology, and pipelines across biotech and pharma are growing quickly. For drug developers, this is an exciting environment, but it is also one that raises the bar for how programs need to be designed and interpreted. Speed alone is not the central challenge, and the question is whether teams can make strong translational decisions early enough to reduce uncertainty before clinical advancement. A program may move quickly through individual study steps, but if the evidence does not clearly show tumor localization, target engagement, biological activity, and a rational dose strategy, that speed can create risk rather than confidence. In radiopharmaceutical development, a fast preclinical package is only valuable when it is also a defensible one. This is where preclinical strategy becomes critical. Why Preclinical Strategy Is Critical for Radiopharmaceutical Programs A strong preclinical package for a radiopharmaceutical agent needs to answer more than whether the compound can be labeled or whether radioactivity can be measured in tissue. It needs to show whether the agent reaches the tumor, whether uptake is selective, whether target expression aligns with biodistribution, and whether the observed signal translates into meaningful efficacy. These data points are not separate outputs. They are connected pieces of the same translational decision, and they need to be planned together from the start. That connection matters because radiopharmaceutical development introduces layers of complexity that traditional oncology studies do not always capture. The isotope, targeting vector, tumor model, expression profile, biodistribution pattern, dosimetry approach, and therapeutic endpoint all influence how a program should be interpreted. If any one of these elements is considered in isolation, it can create an incomplete or misleading picture. A promising uptake result, for example, is difficult to act on without a clear understanding of target expression, exposure, and downstream biology. Using Clinically Relevant PDX Models to Evaluate Radiopharmaceutical Candidates Clinically relevant PDX models are especially valuable in this environment because they help sponsors evaluate radiopharmaceutical candidates in tumor systems that better reflect human disease. PDX models can capture tumor heterogeneity, target-expression variability, stromal architecture, and treatment-response biology in ways that conventional systems may not fully represent. For radiopharmaceutical programs, that biological context can help determine whether uptake is target-associated, whether tumor selectivity is meaningful, and whether efficacy is likely to translate beyond a narrow experimental setting. When PDX data are combined with biodistribution, imaging, and dosimetry, the translational story becomes far more defensible. Planning Radiopharmaceutical Studies Around PDX Growth, Isotope Availability, and Translational Readiness At the same time, radiopharmaceutical programs need to be honest about what drives their timelines. PDX growth kinetics can be variable, isotope availability can affect study scheduling, radiochemistry optimization can require iteration. These are not obstacles to progress, but are simply realities of the modality that need to be reflected in study planning. Preclinical timelines are not just operational timelines - they are biological and chemical timelines that directly shape how confidently a program can advance toward the clinic. This is where a clinically relevant preclinical platform earns its value. Because PDX models retain the tumor heterogeneity, target expression, and treatment-response biology seen in patients, the data generated early in development carries genuine translational weight, helping sponsors anticipate clinical performance rather than simply satisfying a preclinical checkpoint. The opportunity, then, is not simply to move faster but to build preclinical evidence strong enough to translate directly into clinical strategy. Connecting Biodistribution, Dosimetry, Imaging, and Efficacy in Preclinical Radiopharma Studies That requires early alignment on the right models, endpoints, readouts, and study sequence. Biodistribution and dosimetry data need to be interpreted in the context of target expression and imaging should be connected to downstream efficacy. Efficacy results need to be evaluated alongside exposure, selectivity, and tumor biology. Each step should help teams understand whether the agent is behaving as intended, whether the model is answering the intended question, and whether the program has a clear scientific rationale for continued development. When these elements are planned as part of an integrated preclinical strategy, teams can significantly reduce avoidable uncertainty. They can make more confident go/no-go decisions, refine dose rationale, and identify potential risks before they become more costly at later stages. They can also build a stronger translational narrative for internal stakeholders, investors, and clinical development teams, which is increasingly important in a competitive funding environment. Preparing Radiopharmaceutical Programs for Regulatory, Clinical, and Investor Questions There is also a strategic benefit to preparing for downstream questions early. Regulators, clinical collaborators, and investors will eventually ask how the dose was chosen, why a specific tumor context was prioritized, and how the biodistribution data support the therapeutic index. Programs that plan for these questions during preclinical development are better positioned to answer them with clarity rather than reconstruct the story from disconnected studies later. Building Translational Confidence in Radiopharmaceutical Development Radiopharmaceutical development is moving fast, and that momentum is a positive sign for the field. But speed only creates value when it is supported by evidence that is biologically meaningful, operationally reliable, and translationally connected. For teams advancing radiopharmaceutical programs, the real advantage will come from building confidence early, through preclinical strategies that connect chemistry, biology, imaging, and interpretation into a single decision-making framework. Faster progress is welcome. Better decisions are essential. Build confidence in your next radiopharmaceutical development decision.

title: Coaching CRM Without Kajabi Fees (2026): Client Progress Portal You Own
summary: Build a coaching client progress portal without Kajabi fees using Taskade Genesis. Compare against HoneyBook, Notion, and course platforms honestly for 2026.
body_text: Blog AI Coaching CRM Without Kajabi… On this page (21) Taskade Genesis gives coaches a client progress portal, session notes, and homework tracking linked to each client record, without Kajabi LMS fees or course funnels built for creators selling pre-recorded video at scale. This guide compares honest coaching CRM paths in 2026. TL;DR: Kajabi wins video course businesses. HoneyBook wins packaged client intake. Taskade Genesis wins coaches who want a progress portal they own for 1:1 and group programs. Generate a coaching client progress portal → Related: exam prep score tracker no code , client portal builders , Taskade Genesis vs AI app builders , cohort ops without an LMS . A note on prices. This guide deliberately does not print competitor dollar figures. Creator-platform and client-CRM tiers changed more than once through 2025 and 2026, and a stale number is worse than no number. Open each vendor's live pricing page the day you buy, and confirm the tier that actually contains the feature you need. Taskade figures below are current as of July 2026. 🧭 What Coaches Actually Need From a Coaching CRM A coaching CRM needs five things: a client record with goals, a session log, homework with due dates, a check-in trail between sessions, and a login where the client sees their own progress and nothing else. Everything past that — video hosting, affiliate mechanics, launch funnels, checkout pages — is a course-business feature, not a coaching feature. Most coaching weeks look like this: A client books or confirms a session. The session happens, and notes plus action items land somewhere. Homework goes out, scoped to that one client or that one cohort week. Something between sessions either happens or quietly does not. The next session starts with "where did we leave off?" Step five is the whole business. It is also the step that a course platform does not model, because a course platform assumes the content is the product and the learner is self-serve. Daily need All-in-one course platform default Living progress portal you own Client record with goals Contact + purchase history Linked client Project with custom fields Session notes Not a first-class object Session log rows with action items Homework per client Course lesson for everyone Assignment rows with owner and due date Between-session check-ins Email broadcast Async prompts on the client record Client login Course player access Taskade Genesis App Users, scoped per client Pre-recorded video library Native, strong Not its strength — link Loom, Vimeo, Drive Marketing funnels + affiliates Native, strong Not its strength — keep your stack Who renames a field Vendor template You, in a sentence to Taskade EVE If rows one through five are your week, you are shopping for ownership of the record. If rows six and seven are your week, the LMS bill is buying you something real and you should keep it. 📜 Why the LMS Bill Outlived the LMS Need All-in-one creator platforms were priced for a launch, not for a practice. The bundle made sense when the business was "record forty lessons, run a webinar, sell a thousand seats." Video hosting, funnels, email, and checkout in one login was genuinely cheaper than assembling five tools. Three things changed the math for coaches: Delivery moved back to live. Group programs, cohort pods, and 1:1 retainers sell better than evergreen video for many practitioners. Live delivery needs a roster and a progress record, not a player and a funnel. The real system of record drifted into tabs. Goals in a spreadsheet, notes in Docs, homework in chat, invoices in a third tool. The platform kept billing while the daily truth lived somewhere it could not see. Generating a portal got cheap. In 2026 you describe a client progress portal in a sentence and get a working app with linked records and real logins. That moves the decision from "which creator platform?" to "do I rent a schema or own one?" None of this makes Kajabi or Teachable wrong. It makes them priced for a different shape of business than the one many coaches actually run. The tell is simple: open your platform bill, then list the modules you touched last month. If the video library and the funnel builder are not on that list, you are funding capacity you do not use. That loop is the product a coaching CRM should own. Video files and checkout pages are attachments to it. 💵 2026 Pricing Reality: What Your Coaching Stack Actually Funds Compare pricing shapes before you compare numbers, because the shape is what stops fitting as you grow. Seat-priced tools punish adding a second coach. Contact-priced tools punish a big free cohort. Module-gated tools punish needing one feature that sits one tier up. Platform Pricing shape What the price bundles What coaches often never open Kajabi Tiered plan, limits on products and contacts Video hosting, funnels, email, checkout, community Affiliate mechanics, funnel builder, upsell pages Teachable Tiered plan plus transaction handling on lower tiers Course player, checkout, basic email Coaching-specific progress fields, session logs HoneyBook / Dubsado Per-user or flat plan Contracts, invoices, intake forms, scheduling Long-horizon progress tracking across months Notion / Airtable Per-editor seat Flexible database, docs, views Real client logins without permission gymnastics Taskade Genesis Workspace plan, not per-client Projects, AI agents, automations, published apps Nothing you have to buy to get the portal Then run the shape against your own next twelve months: Growth event next year Seat-priced tool Contact-priced platform Workspace plan Add a second coach New paid seat Usually free Covered by the plan's members Add 40 free cohort members Usually free Can push a tier App Users, not editor seats Need a custom field per trade Vendor template limits Vendor template limits Rename it yourself Need one gated feature Upgrade a tier Upgrade a tier Check the plan table once Need a branded domain Often top tiers Often mid or top tier Business plan Taskade pricing, stated plainly. Taskade starts free at $0, and new accounts get a one-time grant of 6,000 credits — 1,000 at signup plus 5,000 with your first build, which is sized to fund one complete app end to end. Pro is $10 per month billed annually, or $20 month to month. Business is $25 per month billed annually, or $50 month to month, and adds custom domain publishing for the portal your clients open. Your video host, checkout, and contracts stay billed wherever they are today. Full detail lives on pricing . 🧬 Workspace DNA: Projects, Agents, Automations A Taskade Genesis coaching portal is not a static template. It runs on Workspace DNA — Memory, Intelligence, and Execution reinforcing each other. Pillar Component Role in a coaching practice Memory Projects Client profiles, goals, session logs, homework, check-in history Intelligence AI Agents Draft check-in prompts, summarize session notes, flag missed homework Execution Automations Send homework reminders, escalate a silent client, post cohort announcements The loop: a closed session writes Memory, an agent reads that Memory and proposes the next check-in, an automation delivers it, and the client's reply writes Memory again. That is why a portal you use daily gets sharper, while a spreadsheet you maintain daily just gets longer. Records live in Projects, so the same client data renders in whichever of the 7 project views fits the moment — Board for program stage, Table for the homework grid, Calendar for session dates, Mind Map for a goal tree, plus List, Gantt, and Org Chart. Access uses Taskade's 7-tier role model from Owner down to Viewer, so an assistant coach can edit session notes without touching billing or program structure. 🗂 The Data Model Behind a Coaching Portal Get the nouns right and the portal survives every program redesign. Get them wrong and you rebuild in month three. Four nouns are non-negotiable: client, session, homework, check-in. Program is the fifth if you run tiers or cohorts. Those entities become the surfaces a client actually sees when they log in: Surface Purpose Example field Client profile Goals, start date, program tier Program tier, renewal date Session log Date, notes, action items Held on, agenda, next step Homework Assignments, due dates, completion Task, due date, status Check-ins Async prompts between sessions Asked on, client answer Resources Links to embedded videos or PDFs Loom link, worksheet file Goal tree Long-horizon outcomes under a theme Outcome, milestone, evidence Cohort field Which run the client belongs to Cohort code, seat status Billing note Link to Stripe or HoneyBook if billing stays external Invoice URL, paid status Feedback End-of-program testimonial capture Rating, quote, consent Read database projects for how linked records behave, and Table view for the grid coaches live in. Client logins come from Taskade Genesis App Users — each client sees only their own records, which is exactly what a shared Notion base cannot do cleanly. Publishing steps are in publishing , branded URLs in custom domains , and email-based sign-in in Taskade Genesis Auth . 🤖 Check-Ins That Do Not Depend on Your Memory The follow-up is where coaching revenue leaks. A client goes quiet in week three, you notice in week five, and the renewal conversation is already lost. Agents fix this by watching the record instead of your calendar. Agents in Taskade come with 34 built-in tools and read the same Projects the portal renders, so a prep note cites real rows rather than guessing. Configure them in custom agents and agent tools , and see agent memory for how context persists across weeks. Automation triggers covers what can start a run, and scheduling covers recurring cadence. Taskade also connects to 100+ integrations bidirectionally — triggers pull events in, actions push data out — so a Stripe payment or a form submission can land on the right client record. Browse integrations for the current list. ✅ Who Should Switch to a Portal They Own Switch, or dual-run, when several of these are true: You run 1:1 retainers or live cohorts , and pre-recorded video is a supporting asset rather than the product. Your current "CRM" is a spreadsheet plus chat , and the pain is progress visibility, not payments. Clients keep asking "where do I see my status?" in DMs. You want custom fields for your niche — lift numbers, interview rounds, macros, sales calls booked — without waiting on a vendor template. You need per-client logins and your current tool only offers all-or-nothing sharing. You want AI follow-ups grounded in your records , not a chatbot that cannot see them. Three genuine strengths per incumbent: Stay on Kajabi when: The video library is the product. Kajabi's hosted player, drip scheduling, and completion tracking are purpose-built for evergreen course delivery. Taskade Genesis does not host an LMS video library and is not trying to. Launch mechanics drive revenue. Funnels, upsells, order bumps, and affiliate tracking in one login is real leverage during a launch week. Rebuilding that across three tools to save a subscription is a bad trade. One bill, one vendor, one support queue. Consolidated billing and a single onboarding path have genuine operational value, especially for a solo creator without an ops person. Stay on HoneyBook or Dubsado when: Contracts and invoices are the workflow. Proposal to signature to payment, with templates and reminders, is their core competency and it is mature. Client intake is the bottleneck. Branded inquiry forms feeding a pipeline with automated follow-up is packaged and proven. Scheduling plus payments must live together. If booking a paid session is one flow for you, splitting it across tools adds failure points. Run parallel, prove the portal on five real clients, then decide. Every member sees it in their own portal; nobody sees anyone else's progress. 17:00 A renewal is 30 days out. The automation already surfaced it, so the conversation happens before the deadline instead of after. Nothing in that day requires an LMS video library or a funnel builder. It requires a record your clients trust and you can reshape. 👥 Group Coaching Without a Second Tool Run cohorts by adding a group field on client records rather than duplicating the whole app per run. Revisit the data model before adding more automations. ❓ FAQ Is Taskade Genesis cheaper than Kajabi for coaches? Total cost depends on your stack. Kajabi bundles video hosting, funnels, and checkout into one price. Taskade starts free at $0, with Pro at $10 per month billed annually ($20 month to month) and Business at $25 per month billed annually ($50 month to month) when you want a custom domain. Keep your course host and checkout, and link them from the record. How do clients log in? Through Taskade Genesis App Users . Each client sees only their own goals, files, messages, and session history — not your workspace. Sign-in is email-based via Taskade Genesis Auth , and Business plans at $25 per month billed annually add publishing on your own domain. Can I embed video homework? Yes, as links or embeds on each client record. Taskade Genesis does not replace a video CDN, so host on Vimeo, Loom, YouTube unlisted, or Drive and link from the portal. Clients open the video from the same record holding their goals and due dates. Does Taskade Genesis handle contracts and payments? Contracts and payments typically stay in HoneyBook, Dubsado, or Stripe beside the portal. Taskade Genesis holds the coaching progress truth. Add a billing-note field that links to the invoice, and sync status through automations if you want payment state visible next to progress. What does the AI actually do for follow-ups? Agents draft check-in prompts, summarize session notes, and flag clients who missed homework before the next session. They read the same Projects the portal renders, so a prep note cites real rows. Start with custom agents and add tools from the 34 built-in tools as you need them. How does this compare to a Notion or Airtable build? Notion and Airtable are excellent shared databases and a reasonable place to start. They struggle at exactly one thing coaches need: a per-client login that shows one client their own records without permission gymnastics. If that is your blocker, read Notion alternative and client portal builders . Do I need to code to build a coaching client portal? No. You describe the portal in a prompt and get client profiles, goals, session history, homework, and check-in status. Rename fields for executive coaching, fitness, or career coaching in plain language. Logins come from App Users, so you never build authentication yourself. What about exam prep coaching? Use the dedicated exam prep score tracker when clients log practice test scores beside session notes and study plans, and read exam prep score tracker no code for the full build. How long does a move actually take? Plan one week to a working pilot and two weeks to trust. Generate on day one, import five clients on day two, backfill two weeks of notes on day three, pilot one login on day four, turn on one automation on day five. Cancel nothing until the old spreadsheet has gained zero new rows for a full week. 📚 Related Reading Cohort ops without an LMS Student enrollment portal without Kajabi Exam prep score tracker, no code Client portal builders compared Build a client portal without code Self-updating client portals Softr alternative: a living client portal Agency client portal templates AI education portals and study tools Agentic CRM: build your own AI CRM without code Taskade Genesis vs AI app builders Taskade Genesis app builder , AI agents , automations , and the Community Gallery 🚀 Own the Record, Pair the Rest Kajabi earned its place by making course businesses possible for people who could not build one. Coaches deserve a second question in 2026: are we buying a course platform, or renting one to store a client record we could own? If your product is a video library and a launch funnel, stay where you are and negotiate with clear eyes. If your product is a relationship measured in sessions, homework, and follow-through, generate the portal and keep video and payments in their lanes. title: BFCM Referral Offers: A Wallet Field Guide
summary: Plan BFCM referral offers customers can save, share, and use with Wallet. A practical guide for Black Friday and Cyber Monday campaigns.
body_text: All Posts >> BFCM Referral Offers: A Wallet Field Guide Referral Marketing Wallet Pass BFCM Referral Offers: A Wallet Field Guide Jeremy Foreshew Head of Marketing & Partnerships at Talkable Jeremy Foreshew Head of Marketing & Partnerships at Talkable 11 hours ago 4 min read Talkable Wallet / BFCM field guide A referral offer customers can keep. Use Wallet to make BFCM referral offers easier to save, find again, and send when the sale is live. Black Friday and Cyber Monday referral campaigns have a familiar problem: customers see an offer, mean to come back, then lose it in the noise. A digital Wallet pass gives the friend offer, earned reward, and next action a home on the phone. It is there when a customer is ready to share or shop. This is a practical guide for teams planning BFCM referral offers with Talkable Wallet , Apple Wallet, and Google Wallet. A Wallet pass keeps the active referral offer and reward close at hand. The idea: make the offer feel kept, not chased Inbox placement is fragile during BFCM. A referral offer that gets saved to Wallet has another way back to the customer when they are ready to shop. The point is simple. Give the offer a home on the phone, then give people a reason to reopen it. Wallet works best when it gives the customer a usable offer, not another reason to open an email. The sale is loud. The offer should be easy to keep. The customer motion A Wallet offer has a job at each point in the sale. 01 / Save it Give people something worth holding onto before BFCM starts: early access, a live referral reward, or a friend offer with a real end date. 02 / Find it again Put the current offer and customer reward where they can see them in a second. Wallet should be the fast route back to value. 03 / Send it Prompt customers who saved but have not shared. Tie the reminder to the sale, not to an automated follow-up cadence. 04 / Use it Bring earned rewards back when the deadline actually matters. If there is no value left, leave the customer alone. Wallet can carry the customer from saving an offer to sharing and reward use. Message direction Pass updates for Black Friday and Cyber Monday Every update needs a reason to exist. Keep the copy close to the customer’s actual moment. The pass is useful when it says what changed and what to do next. 01 / AFTER SAVE Confirm the offer is there. “Your BFCM referral offer is saved. Share it with a friend and keep your reward ready for the sale.” 02 / BLACK FRIDAY Make the live offer obvious. “Black Friday is on. Open Wallet to see your referral offer and reward.” 03 / FINAL HOURS Bring an earned reward back. “Your reward is still in Wallet. Use it before the offer expires.” Use pass updates for live offer changes, referral prompts, and expiration messages. Skip generic reminders. Build the pass as campaign creative A Wallet pass is a small campaign asset, not a tiny website. The pass needs to make the offer clear, keep the next action close, and give customers a reason to come back. Put the value first. Lead with the reward or the friend offer. No decoding required. Make BFCM visible. Give the pass event-specific creative, language, and a real end date. Keep the action close. Sharing, referral information, and useful links should be easy to find. Campaign calendar The BFCM operating rhythm Plan around the sale, not around the feature. 01 BEFORE BFCM Earn the save. Introduce Wallet as a place to hold early access or a live referral offer before the event begins. 02 FRIDAY Make the offer unmistakable. Update the pass so the current reward and customer action are clear at a glance. 03 WEEKEND Make sharing timely. Talk to customers who saved but have not shared. Make the live event the reason to act. 04 LAST CALL Make reward use easy. Bring active, unused rewards back before the deadline. Do not create urgency where there is no value left. The filter for every update: does the customer have a real reason to act right now? What to measure in a Wallet referral campaign An install is the start. The next action is the signal. Watch how customers move from install to share, reward use, and Wallet-attributed sales. That is where the campaign earns its place in the BFCM plan. Install rate First referral share Reward redemption Wallet-attributed sales For more on how Wallet can connect referral activity to customer action, read Talkable’s guide to Wallet attribution . If Wallet makes the offer easier to keep and easier to use, it is doing its job. Frequently asked questions about BFCM referral offers What is a Wallet referral offer? It is a referral offer or reward that a customer saves to Apple Wallet or Google Wallet. The pass can show the current value and give the customer a direct route to share or shop. When should a brand ask customers to save a Wallet pass? Ask when the pass holds a specific benefit worth keeping, such as early access, a referral offer, a reward, or an event-related incentive. How often should brands update a pass during BFCM? Only when there is a real change the customer can use. Black Friday launch, a distinct Cyber Monday offer, and a valid reward deadline are sensible moments. Repeated generic reminders are not. What should brands measure? Measure movement from install to share, reward use, referral conversion, and attributed sales. Review profitability and quality signals alongside volume. title: Maintenance Knowledge Loss: Why Hiring Does Not Replace a Retiring Technician
summary: Why hiring a replacement technician does not restore what a retiring one knew, and how capturing, connecting, and surfacing asset history closes the gap.
body_text: Maintenance Knowledge Loss: Why Hiring Does Not Replace a Retiring Technician Maintenance knowledge loss happens when a technician's undocumented understanding of how specific equipment behaves leaves the plant with them. Hiring a replacement restores the hours but not the record. Closing that gap takes three capabilities: capturing knowledge at the point of work, connecting each record to the asset, and surfacing that history before anyone needs it. The standard story about manufacturing today points to a labor shortage. Not enough skilled people, an aging workforce, a hiring market that cannot keep up. All of that holds true, and none of it tells the whole story. Fully staffed plants still lose hours to failures a retired technician would have caught in minutes, because that person's expertise never made it into a system anyone else could find. Why do fully staffed plants still lose hours to unplanned downtime? Fully staffed plants still lose hours to unplanned downtime because headcount and knowledge are separate assets. A plant can replace a retiring technician's shifts and still lose the only record of how a specific machine behaves before it fails. Deloitte and The Manufacturing Institute project a net need for 3.8 million U.S. manufacturing jobs by 2033, of which roughly 2.8 million open through retirement rather than growth. Picture a Monday-morning leadership meeting covering the same three problems it covered last week, and the week before that. One production line keeps going down for reasons nobody can fully explain. A senior technician just handed in a two-week notice, and no one is sure how the plant runs without them. The new hire has been on the floor for three weeks and still does not know who to call when something breaks. None of this means your team lacks skill or effort. The system they are working from quietly depends on a few veterans knowing the answers by heart, and that system no longer matches the plant floor in front of them. Does this sound like your weekly leadership meeting? "We're short-staffed again this quarter." "We lost another senior tech and nobody documented what he knew." "The new hire doesn't know where anything is or who to call." "We have the data, we just don't have time to use it." "We keep hiring, and we're still behind." What is tribal knowledge in maintenance? Tribal knowledge in maintenance is operating understanding that exists only in a technician's memory. It covers how a machine sounds before it fails, why a procedure contains a particular step, and which fix holds under load. Tribal knowledge is undocumented, unattached to any asset record, and untransferable. When the technician leaves, the knowledge leaves with them. The median manufacturing worker is 44.5 years old against 41.9 across all industries, and the share of plants where a quarter or more of the workforce is 55 or older has climbed sharply since 2000. That aging curve is becoming an exit wave, and each departure takes more than headcount. What actually leaves runs deeper than a job title. The knowledge that keeps equipment running was never written down anywhere durable. It lives as a mental catalog of how each machine behaves, as a note scrawled on a work order, as something said once during a shift change and never repeated. The person leaves, and the record goes with them. The gap this creates is now blocking the technology meant to close it. In a 2026 survey of 300 manufacturing professionals by Redwood Software, 98% of manufacturers reported exploring or considering AI-driven automation while only 20% said they were fully prepared to scale it. Models and dashboards need a clean record of what happened to which asset and why. Most plants do not have one. How much does undocumented maintenance knowledge cost a plant? Undocumented maintenance knowledge costs a plant the gap between average wrench time and top-performer wrench time. Wrench time is the share of a shift a technician spends working on equipment rather than searching for information or waiting on parts. Industry average sits at 25 to 35 percent against 55 to 65 percent for top performers, and most of that gap is time spent looking for something a colleague already knew. Here is how to calculate what the gap costs you: (hours lost per technician per week to information search) × (technician count) × (loaded hourly rate) × (52 weeks) = annual cost of the knowledge gap Run it once at plant level and the number is uncomfortable. Multiply it across a portfolio and it becomes a line item worth defending in front of a board. What happens when a preventive maintenance step goes undocumented? A preventive maintenance step that goes undocumented keeps getting marked complete while the underlying work stops happening. The PM record shows compliance and the failure rate shows something else, and nobody connects the two because no single record holds both. Turnover makes it permanent. Once the people who remembered the step are gone, the written procedure becomes the only surviving version of the truth. Picture a mid-size plant that is profitable, well run, with no red flags on paper. For months, one line keeps going down for the same failure, and every time the fix looks routine enough that nobody digs deeper. The preventive maintenance schedule for that line was being marked complete every time. What the record did not show was that a lubrication step had quietly dropped out of the routine months earlier during a busy stretch, and was never added back. With high turnover, the newer technicians were following the written PM exactly as documented, and no one left on the team remembered the step that was missing. It was only when the failures became too frequent and too expensive to write off that someone finally noticed. That is when leadership stopped asking who do we hire next? and started asking a better question: how do we capture what this technician knew, tie it to the equipment, and put it in front of the next person before they guess wrong? How do you capture institutional knowledge in maintenance? Capturing institutional knowledge in maintenance takes three capabilities, and they work on any platform. Capture at the point of work records what happened while the technician still remembers the specifics. Connecting the record to the asset builds one running history per piece of equipment. Surfacing that history at the machine puts it in front of the next person before they guess. Capture at the point of work Capture at the point of work is documentation that happens during or immediately after the job, while the details that fade fastest are still available. Most plants already ask technicians to document their work, but timing trips them up. A note written three days after a repair, from memory, during a slow moment between other jobs, bears little resemblance to one written in the first ten minutes after the fix. Right after the repair, the technician remembers the unusual sound the bearing made before it failed, that the standard fix did not hold and they had to improvise a second approach, and the exact torque that felt wrong. None of that survives a week of memory and a dozen other work orders in between. Capturing those specifics, rather than "replaced bearing," is what separates a closed ticket from a record that teaches the next person something. Connect the record to the asset Record-to-asset connection is the practice of attaching every failure, fix, part, and procedure permanently to a specific piece of equipment rather than to a work order that closes. A plant can have excellent individual notes and still have no institutional memory, because those notes are scattered. The work order lands in the CMMS, the safety procedure lives in a binder in the supervisor's office, and the diagnostic history goes unrecorded anywhere. Three people can service the same pump over many months and each treats it as a brand-new problem, because none of them can see what the others already tried. Once records connect, patterns surface on their own. A pump that has failed the same way four times in eight months poses a completely different diagnostic problem than a pump failing for the first time, but only if someone can see all four failures in one place. Without that connection, a plant relearns the same lesson every time, at full cost, with no memory of having paid for it before. Surface it before it is needed Surfacing is making an asset's history available at the machine, on the device the technician already carries, within the first minutes of a stoppage. A new hire standing in front of a stopped machine makes a decision quickly. They will try the obvious fix, call someone, or troubleshoot from scratch. If the equipment's history is on their phone right then, they inherit the last technician's judgment instead of guessing blind. If it is not, they might spend an hour re-testing a fix that someone already confirmed did not work six months earlier. A history that is technically documented somewhere but takes fifteen minutes and a call to a supervisor to track down might as well not exist for the person standing at the machine right now. Capture → Connect → Surface. Plants that build these three habits, on any platform, hold onto what a retiring technician knew long after that technician is gone. What does a CMMS need in order to retain institutional knowledge? A CMMS retains institutional knowledge when capture, connection, and visibility are built into the daily work of opening and closing a work order rather than bolted on as a separate documentation project. UpKeep is the CMMS platform trusted by 4,000+ companies to manage maintenance, safety, and reliability, bringing work orders, preventive maintenance, and asset history onto one platform so teams can drive a 26%+ decrease in downtime and an 11% increase in asset life. Most plants already own the raw materials. A shared drive for manuals, a spreadsheet for PM schedules, and people who know the equipment cold. What is lacking is the connection between them. So when a newer technician stands in front of a stopped asset, whatever would help arrives too late to matter, assuming it arrives at all. Running the three capabilities on one system is what closes that distance. In UpKeep CMMS, every work order, asset record, safety procedure, and training module ties to the same piece of equipment: Capture at the point of work. Log work from a phone in the field. Built-in AI turns a spoken note or a photographed ticket into a structured work order that records the cause, the fix, and the parts used while the details are still fresh. Connect the record to the asset. Every entry ties to the specific asset, building one running history of failures, fixes, cost, and procedures in one place. Surface it before it is needed. That history is visible from any phone at the point of work, and a proven fix can become a standard procedure the next technician inherits. The plant described above never lacked another hire. What it lacked was anything linking the repeated failures to the incomplete PM. Once connected reporting tied the two together, the missing step surfaced on its own. Where should a plant start? A plant should start by measuring where knowledge is leaking today, before designing any documentation program. Identify the assets where retirement risk and criticality overlap, check whether their history is captured, connected, and visible, and use that one line as the baseline for everything else. A fifteen-minute reliability audit maps this against your own equipment. The labor shortage is real, and hiring faster is the slower way to protect your plant floor. The faster way is making sure that when your most experienced people retire, what they knew stays behind. Download the full playbook here .
