title: How to track buyer intent in B2B SaaS in 2026
summary: A 6-step framework for tracking buyer intent in B2B SaaS: define signals, choose sources, build scoring, route to reps, automate, and measure.
body_text: Article overview Tracking buyer intent is a six-step build, not a single tool purchase: define, source, score, route, act, measure. Most programs fail at step 3 (scoring) or step 5 (automatic action), not at step 2 (buying enough signal sources). Contact-level resolution and custom scoring are what separate a working program from a dashboard nobody opens. The build works the same at $20M ARR or $500M ARR; only the volume and org structure around it change. Introduction "How do we track buyer intent" usually gets answered with a vendor name. That's a step-2 answer to a six-step question. Teams that buy a signal source and stop there end up with exactly what the pipeline-gap research keeps finding: a dashboard that shows accounts spiking, and no reliable path from that spike to a closed deal. This is the build, in order. Skipping a step doesn't save time, it just moves the failure downstream to a step that's more expensive to fix. 6 steps to track buyer intent Step 1: Define what "intent" means for your buyers Before choosing a signal source, define what a real buying signal looks like for your specific ICP. A visit to a comparison page from a named account in your target list is a different signal than a spike in generic blog traffic from an unknown visitor. Map signals to your actual buying stages (awareness, evaluation, decision) instead of treating every behavior as equally warm. Skipping this step is why so many programs end up scoring noise. Step 2: Choose signal sources deliberately Most programs default to third-party keyword/topic intent (a vendor's panel data showing a company is researching a category) because it's the easiest to buy. The stronger mix layers in first-party signals: website de-anonymization down to the individual visitor, product usage if you have a freemium or trial motion, and buying-committee activity across a target account. First-party signals are typically higher-fidelity because they're your own visitors doing something on your own property, not an inference from panel data. Step 3: Build or select a scoring model trained on your own history This is where most programs quietly fail. An off-the-shelf, industry-wide scoring model assumes every company's buyers behave the same way. A model trained on your own closed-won and closed-lost history will weight signals the way your actual sales history says to weight them, which is the difference between a score reps trust and one they learn to ignore after the second false positive. Step 4: Resolve signals to a named contact and route them An account-level score tells a rep a company is active. A contact-level score tells them who, with a reason attached, at least at enterprise scale where the average buying committee runs 11 stakeholders per Gartner. Routing logic needs to reflect who's actually positioned to act, not just a static CRM ownership field. Step 5: Automate the action, not just the alert A scored, named contact should generate a next step on its own, a drafted email, a CRM task, a synced ad audience, without a rep needing to notice the alert first. This is the step that turns "we track intent" into "intent turns into pipeline," and it's the step most legacy intent tools were never built to do, because they were built as reporting layers. Step 6: Measure pipeline and revenue impact, not signal volume The most common mistake in reporting on an intent program is measuring how many signals fired instead of how many turned into logged outreach, meetings, and pipeline. Do we need first-party and third-party intent signals, or just one? A mix is stronger. title: Gucci Bloom Ambrosia di Fiori vs Gucci Bloom: Which Should You Wear?
summary: Gucci Bloom Ambrosia di Fiori vs Gucci Bloom: green and dewy or rosy and honeyed? The real difference, and how to try both on Scentbird.
body_text: Gucci Bloom Ambrosia di Fiori usually gets summed up as Bloom with the volume turned up, and that shortcut sells both perfumes short. The real Gucci Bloom Ambrosia di Fiori vs Gucci Bloom question is not stronger versus weaker. It is whether you want your white flowers green and dewy, or deepened into rose and honey, because that is the actual choice Ambrosia di Fiori puts in front of you. Gucci Bloom Ambrosia di Fiori, available to try on Scentbird. Ambrosia di Fiori vs Gucci Bloom: the similarities Family resemblance runs deep here, and no wonder: both come from the same nose. Both are unapologetic white florals with tuberose and jasmine at heart, both skip the usual sparkling-citrus overture and dive straight into petals, and both wear like a statement rather than an afterthought. If white flowers are not your thing, neither bottle will convert you. If they are, the choice between them comes down to light. Gucci Bloom The original Gucci Bloom , composed by Alberto Morillas in 2017, is a white floral in the most literal sense. You step straight into tuberose, jasmine, and Rangoon creeper, and the whole thing smells like a florist’s cool back room, cut stems, white petals, and damp greenery included. What makes it modern is what Morillas left out: no vanilla cushion, no candied edge, so the flowers stay green and watery from the first hour to the last. It projects confidently for the first couple of hours, then wears closer for a total of about seven to nine. Its one genuine risk is the tuberose itself, which can turn heady in a warm, crowded room and reads distinctly bridal to some noses. Skip it if white florals have ever felt like a wedding bouquet you did not order. Gucci Bloom Ambrosia di Fiori Ambrosia di Fiori, Morillas again in 2019, starts from the same bouquet and then changes the light. Damask rose and orange blossom move into the heart, and a honeyed warmth settles underneath, so the same flowers now read as if the garden had shifted to dusk. Where Bloom stays linear and airy, Ambrosia evolves: the rose swells through the middle hours and the finish turns plush and faintly sweet, clinging to scarves and collars well into the next morning. It is the stronger performer at roughly eight to ten hours with a heavier trail. The trade-off is exactly that density. In summer heat or a small office it can feel stifling, and the honeyed finish may frustrate you if you love your florals crisp. Skip it if dewy and green is the whole reason you liked Bloom in the first place. Ambrosia di Fiori vs Gucci Bloom: notes, longevity, and projection Ambrosia di Fiori Gucci Bloom Feel Warm, rosy, honeyed white floral Cool, dewy, green white floral Main notes Tuberose, jasmine, Damask rose, orange blossom Tuberose, jasmine, Rangoon creeper Lasts About 8 to 10 hours, heavier trail About 7 to 9 hours, lighter after opening Best for Evenings, cool weather, occasions Daytime, spring, the office Which one is better, Ambrosia di Fiori or Gucci Bloom? The differentiator is not volume, it is temperature. Bloom is green water; Ambrosia is warm nectar. That one distinction answers most practical questions before they get asked: mornings, offices, and warm afternoons belong to Bloom, while dinners, cold evenings, and nights you want the fragrance to outlast the event belong to Ambrosia. Owning both is not redundant, either, since they cover opposite halves of the same floral year. The short answer Choose Gucci Bloom if you want white flowers kept fresh, green, and easy to wear anywhere in daylight. Choose Ambrosia di Fiori if you want the same bouquet deepened with rose and honey for evenings and cooler months, and do not mind it announcing itself. If you are still torn between them, wearing each for a few days is the quickest way to settle it, and both are on Scentbird, so the comparison can happen on your skin rather than on paper. Give it a full month on your skin before you commit to a bottle. Try Ambrosia di Fiori with Scentbird Prefer the original? Add Gucci Bloom to your queue and wear them back to back. New to Scentbird? Take the fragrance quiz . Frequently asked questions What does Gucci Bloom smell like? Gucci Bloom is a white floral built on tuberose, jasmine, and Rangoon creeper. There is no citrus introduction; it opens straight into cool, dewy petals and stays there, airy and green rather than sweet, like standing in a florist’s back room among cut stems and damp greenery. What does Gucci Bloom Ambrosia di Fiori smell like? Ambrosia di Fiori takes Bloom’s tuberose and jasmine and deepens them with Damask rose and orange blossom over a honeyed base. The effect is the same garden at dusk: warmer, rosier, and noticeably sweeter, with a rich finish that lingers on clothes into the next day. What is the difference between Gucci Bloom and Ambrosia di Fiori? The rose and the honey. Bloom keeps its white flowers green, watery, and fresh from start to finish. Ambrosia di Fiori pours warmth over the same bouquet, so the drydown turns honeyed and plush instead of dewy. Think green water versus warm nectar and you have the difference. Which lasts longer, Bloom or Ambrosia di Fiori? Ambrosia di Fiori. As the intense version it runs about eight to ten hours with a heavier trail, while the original Bloom sits around seven to nine and wears lighter after its strong opening. On fabric, Ambrosia can still be there the next morning. Is Ambrosia di Fiori good for the office? Use a light hand. Its density and honeyed sweetness can feel like a lot in a small, warm room, so one spray is plenty for shared spaces. The original Bloom is the easier office pick because it stays airier and greener through the day. Is Gucci Bloom better for summer? Mostly yes. Its dewy, green character suits mild and warm days, though in real heat and a packed room the tuberose can turn heady, so spray lightly. Ambrosia di Fiori is happier in cool weather and after dark, where its honeyed depth has room to breathe. Related reading: Gucci Bloom vs Gucci Guilty .
